article.html:
The ankh is a word you can wear. Most symbols stand for something; the ankh simply is the word "life" in one of the world's oldest scripts, and Egyptians drew it the way we write a word on a birthday card. On temple walls the gods hold it out by its loop like a key, and the king breathes it in. Life, in Egyptian thinking, is not something you have but something you are given, again and again.

Its shape invites guesses. Is it a sandal strap, a knot, a mirror, a key? Egyptologists still disagree, and perhaps the Egyptians themselves did not think about it: they used the sign because it sounded like the word. But its form proved irresistible to later ages. To the Copts it was the Cross with a circle of eternity; to Renaissance mystics a key to forbidden wisdom; to the twentieth century a badge of rebellion, heritage and darkness all at once.

It is one of the few ancient sacred signs that slipped smoothly into Christianity without a fight. When Egyptians converted, they did not have to give up the sign of life; they simply gave it a new name.

For a storyteller the ankh is a reminder that a symbol can be a sound before it is an idea. A god holding out life on a loop of string is an image older than any myth told about it.

lifetime.html: The sign is found from the beginning of Egyptian writing (c. 3000 BCE) to the end of pagan Egypt. Amulets, mirror cases (one in Tutankhamun's tomb is shaped like an ankh), furniture and jewellery used it. The ankh travelled with Egyptian art into the Levant and Nubia.wp

Egyptian Christians (Copts) adopted the looped cross, the crux ansata, as a form of the Christian cross; it appears on Coptic textiles, carvings and manuscripts from late antiquity. The church historian Socrates Scholasticus reports that when the Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed (391 CE), Christians and pagans alike read the cross-shaped signs found there as meaning "the life to come".wp
European travellers and scholars, fascinated by hieroglyphs they could not yet read, treated the ankh as a mystical "key of life". Champollion's decipherment (1822) confirmed that it meant "life".wp

In the 1960s and 70s the ankh became a sign of the counterculture and of Black pride and African heritage, worn by musicians and activists. It is also popular in goth fashion and in modern Kemetic religion, which revives the worship of the Egyptian gods.wp

myth.html:
In Egyptian writing the sign stood for the word ꜥnḫ, "life", and for other words with similar sounds, such as "mirror" and "sandal strap". In temple and tomb art gods carry it, pour streams of little ankhs over the king as purifying water, or hold it to his face so that he breathes in life. It appears in personal names, such as Tutankhamun, "living image of Amun".wp

No myth tells how the ankh was made: it is a sign rather than an object with a story. It often appears with two other signs, the djed pillar (stability) and the was sceptre (power), forming a wish for life, stability and dominion.wp

blue.overview: Blue is one of the three primary colours in the RGB (additive) colour model, as well as in the RYB colour model (traditional colour theory). It lies between violet and cyan on the spectrum of visible light. The term blue generally describes colours perceived by humans observing light with a dominant wavelength between approximately 450 and 495 nanometres. The clear daytime sky and the deep sea appear blue because of an optical effect known as Rayleigh scattering. An optical effect called the Tyndall effect explains blue eyes. Distant objects appear more blue because of another optical effect called aerial perspective.

green-man.overview: The Green Man, also known as a foliate head, is a motif in architecture and art, of a face made of, or completely surrounded by, foliage, which normally spreads out from the centre of the face. Apart from a purely decorative function, the Green Man is primarily interpreted as a symbol of rebirth, representing the cycle of new growth that occurs every spring. The Green Man motif has many variations. Branches or vines may sprout from the mouth, nostrils, or other parts of the face, and these shoots may bear flowers or fruit. Found in many cultures from many ages around the world, the Green Man is often related to natural vegetation deities.

megingjord.overview: In Norse mythology, the megingjörð (Old Norse: megingjǫrð [ˈmeɣenˌɡjɔrð], meaning "power-belt") is a belt worn by the god Thor. The Old Norse name megin means power or strength, and gjörð means belt. According to the Prose Edda, the belt is one of Thor's three main possessions, along with the hammer Mjölnir and the iron gloves Járngreipr. When worn, the belt is described as doubling Thor's already prodigious strength. In verse seven of the skaldic poem Þórsdrápa (Thorsdrapa, Lay of Thor) written by the 10th-century poet Eilífr Goðrúnarson, in the service of Jarl Hákon Sigurðarson, refers to Thor's power-belt.

mistletoe.overview: Mistletoe is the common name for obligate hemiparasitic plants in the order Santalales. They are attached to their host tree or shrub by a structure called the haustorium, through which they extract water and nutrients from the host plant. There are hundreds of species which mostly live in tropical regions. The name mistletoe originally referred to the species Viscum album (European mistletoe, of the family Santalaceae in the order Santalales); it is the only species native to the British Isles and much of Europe.

nandaka.overview: Nandaka (Sanskrit: नन्दक, lit. 'source of joy') or Nandaki is the sword of the Hindu god Vishnu. Nandaka is generally depicted in images where Vishnu is represented with more than his usual four arms. The sword is compared to knowledge in Hindu scriptures. In Sri Vaishnavism (a major Vaishnava tradition), the saints Annamacharya and Peyalvar are considered to be the avatars of Nandaka.

sword-of-laban.overview: Laban () is a figure in the First Book of Nephi, near the start of the Book of Mormon, a scripture of the Latter Day Saint movement. Although he only makes a brief appearance in the Book of Mormon, his brass plates play an important role when they are taken by Laman and Nephi (often referred to as the "sons of Lehi") and are used by the Nephites.
sword-of-laban.list_note: After nearly being killed by a powerful and nefarious Laban, the young prophet Nephi later finds him drunk and unconscious. He's then commanded of God to use Laban's sword to kill him as he was wicked and would hurt future generations by withholding sacred records revealing God's Plan of Happiness. The sword was made of "precious steel" with a hilt of "pure gold". After slaying Laban, Nephi put on Laban's armor to disguise himself to obtain the records, and escape the city. He would later use it as a model for manufacturing similar weapons for his people's defense. Laban's sword was passed down through the centuries to future prophets, kings, and warriors.

article.html:
Yggdrasil is a tree that hurts. That is the detail that makes it unforgettable. The gods meet in council under its branches, the Norns weave fate at its feet, and yet "the ash Yggdrasil suffers more than men know": a dragon gnaws its roots, stags strip its leaves, its trunk rots at the side. The world is held together by something wounded, and kept alive only by daily care. Every morning the Norns pour water and white clay over it.

The tree is also a network. A squirrel runs its whole height, from the eagle at the top to the dragon at the bottom, carrying insults. It is a comic detail, and a profound one: the parts of the world are connected even by their quarrels. Information, enmity and fate all travel up and down the same trunk.

Odin's ordeal makes the tree a place of knowledge. He hangs on it for nine nights, wounded, "given to myself", until he sees the runes and takes them up. Wisdom here is not studied but suffered; the god pays with his own life to gain it. Whether or not the poem knew the story of the Crucifixion, it understood that the axis of the world is also a place of sacrifice.

And at the end, when the wolf is loose and the gods are dying, the old tree trembles but does not quite fall. In Snorri's telling two humans hide in the wood and come out into a green, new world.

For a storyteller, Yggdrasil is a model of a setting that is also a character: a world with a centre that can be climbed, wounded, watered and, at the end, survived.

  • "Yew pillar". From an older word for yew, with the tree as a cosmic column.wp
  • "Terror tree". From yggr, terror, without reference to Odin.wp

lifetime.html: Sacred trees and groves were part of Germanic religion from Roman times; the historian Tacitus (1st century CE) describes rites in holy groves.wp

The Saxon sacred pillar Irminsul, perhaps also a world-pillar, was destroyed by Charlemagne in 772. Adam of Bremen (c. 1070) describes a great evergreen tree and a well beside the pagan temple at Uppsala. The Eddic poems that name Yggdrasil were written down in thirteenth-century Iceland, two centuries after the conversion.wp
Scandinavian scholars published the Eddas, and the World Ash entered European learning; a seventeenth-century Icelandic manuscript drawing of the tree is one of the first images of it.wp

The Romantic and nationalist revivals painted and sang of the World Ash; Wagner's Ring opens with the Norns weaving at the ash's foot. In the twentieth century Yggdrasil became a central symbol of Heathenry and a favourite image in fantasy, games and tattoos.wp

myth.html:
The Völuspá, the seeress's prophecy in the Poetic Edda, sees "an ash called Yggdrasil", ever green, standing over the well of Urd, where the three Norns shape the lives of men. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (c. 1220) gives it three roots: one among the gods over the well of Urd, one among the frost giants over Mímir's well of wisdom, and one in Niflheim over the spring Hvergelmir, where the dragon Níðhöggr gnaws it.poeticprose

The tree is alive with creatures. An eagle sits in its top with a hawk between its eyes; the squirrel Ratatoskr runs up and down carrying insults between the eagle and the dragon; four stags browse its leaves; snakes gnaw its roots. The Norns pour water and white clay from the well over it every day so that it does not rot. The poem Grímnismál says the tree suffers more than anyone knows.poeticprose

In the Hávamál Odin tells how he hung on a windswept tree for nine nights, wounded by a spear, given to himself, and then reached down and took up the runes. The name Yggdrasil is often read as "Ygg's horse", Ygg being one of Odin's names and "horse" an old poetic word for the gallows.poeticwp

At Ragnarök, the Völuspá says, the ancient tree trembles and groans. Snorri adds that two humans, Líf and Lífþrasir, will hide in "Hoddmímir's wood" and survive to repeople the earth.poeticprose

seen.html: A living, suffering axis that holds the worlds together: watered by fate (the Norns), gnawed by destruction, and connecting gods, giants, humans and the dead.poeticprose

Mircea Eliade made the world tree a classic example of the axis mundi, the centre where heaven, earth and underworld meet, and compared it with shamanic trees climbed by Siberian shamans. See the reference books' readings of the World Tree and World Axis.wp
Some scholars have read Odin hanging on the tree and wounded by a spear as shaped by the Crucifixion; others defend it as a pagan myth that Christians later found strikingly familiar.wp
